items.label: section_header
items.text: EXTENSION WORK

items.label: text
items.text: The reason that the melting points decrease is that the atoms get bigger as we go down the group. In the metallic lattice, the nuclei of the positive ions are further from the delocalised electrons in caesium than in sodium and therefore there is weaker electrostatic attraction.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 11.4 Lithium, sodium and potassium have to be kept in oil to stop them reacting with oxygen in the air.

items.label: text
items.text: The melting and boiling points of the elements are very low for metals, and get lower as you move down the group.

items.label: text
items.text: Their densities tend to increase down the group, although not regularly. Lithium, sodium and potassium are all less dense than water, and so will float on it.

items.label: text
items.text: The metals are also very soft and are easily cut with a knife, becoming softer as you move down the group. They are shiny and silver when freshly cut, but tarnish very quickly on exposure to air.

items.label: section_header
items.text: STORAGE AND HANDLING

items.label: text
items.text: All these metals are extremely reactive and get more reactive as you go down the group. They all react quickly with oxygen in the air to form oxides, and react rapidly with water to form strongly alkaline solutions of the metal hydroxides. This is why the Group 1 metals are commonly known as the alkali metals.

items.label: text
items.text: To stop them reacting with oxygen or water vapour in the air, lithium, sodium and potassium are stored under oil. Rubidium and caesium are so reactive that they have to be stored in sealed glass tubes to stop any possibility of oxygen getting at them.

items.label: text
items.text: Great care must be taken not to touch any of these metals with bare fingers. There could be enough sweat on your skin to give a reaction, producing lots of heat and a verycorrosive metal hydroxide.

items.label: section_header
items.text: DID YOU KNOW?

items.label: text
items.text: Historically alkali metals were put in the same group because of similarities in properties, before anyone knew anything

items.label: text
items.text: about electrons!

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEYPOINT

items.label: text
items.text: 'M' simply represents any one of the alkali metals. 'X' represents any one of the halogens.

items.label: section_header
items.text: A FAMILY OF ELEMENTS

items.label: text
items.text: There are two reasons that we put these elements in Group 1:

items.label: list_item
items.text: 1 They all have one electron in their outer shell. The electronic configurations are:

items.label: list_item
items.text: 2They have similar chemical properties, for example:

items.label: list_item
items.text: they all react with water (this will be discussed below) in the same way to form a hydroxide with the formula MOH (e.g. LiOH, NaOH)and hydrogen

items.label: list_item
items.text: they react with oxygen to form an oxide with the formula M2O (Na2O, K2O)

items.label: list_item
items.text: they react with halogens to form compounds with the formula MX (e.g. LiCl, KBr)

items.label: list_item
items.text: they form ionic compounds which contain an M+ ion (e.g. Na+, K+).

items.label: text
items.text: The chemical properties depend on the number of electrons in the outer shell. The Group 1 elements react in very similar ways because they all have the same number of electrons in the outer shell (one), so reason 2 is really just a consequence of reason 1.

items.label: text
items.text: We will discuss the chemical properties in more detail below.
